entries.0fb6b030786c5bf5874ba0985299b7025a9e6e70: <div sID="gen11536" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="63" osisID="Ps.63" sID="Ps.63"/> <div eID="gen11536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11537" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11538" type="x-p"/> This psalm has in it as much of warmth and lively devotion as any of David's psalms in so little a compass. As the sweetest of Paul's epistles were those that bore date out of a prison, so some of the sweetest of David's psalms were those that were penned, as this was, in a wilderness. That which grieved him most in his banishment was the want of public ordinances; these he here longs to be restored to the enjoyment of; and the present want did but whet his appetite. Yet it is not the ordinances, but the God of the ordinances, that his heart is upon. And here we have, I. His desire towards God, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His esteem of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.3-Ps.63.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. His satisfaction in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">ver. 5</reference>. IV. His secret communion with God, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.6">ver. 6</reference>. V. His joyful dependence upon God, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.7-Ps.63.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. IV. His holy triumph in God over his enemies and in the assurance of his own safety, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.9-Ps.63.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. A devout and pious soul has little need of direction how to sing this psalm, so naturally does it speak its own genuine language; and an unsanctified soul, that is unacquainted and unaffected with divine things, is scarcely capable of singing it with understanding.
entries.c120bf7f41d83ec1ef6bc216aa695b63d0fe2e95: <div eID="gen11538" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11537" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Affections.</title> <div sID="gen11539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O God, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is; <hi type="super">2</hi> To see thy power and thy glory, so <hi type="italic">as</hi> I have seen thee in the sanctuary. <div eID="gen11539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11540" type="x-p"/> The title tells us when the psalm was penned, when David was <hi type="italic">in the wilderness of Judah;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">in the forest of Hareth</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">1 Sam. xxii. 5</reference>) or in <hi type="italic">the wilderness of Ziph,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15">1 Sam. xxiii. 15</reference>. 1. Even in Canaan, though a fruitful land and the people numerous, yet there were wildernesses, places less fruitful and less inhabited than other places. It will be so in the world, in the church, but not in heaven; there it is all city, all paradise, and no desert ground; <hi type="italic">the wilderness</hi> there <hi type="italic">shall blossom as the rose.</hi> 2. The best and dearest of God's saints and servants may sometimes have their lot cast in a wilderness, which speaks them lonely and solitary, desolate and afflicted, wanting, wandering, and unsettled, and quite at a loss what to do with themselves. 3. All the straits and difficulties of a wilderness must not put us out of tune for sacred songs; but even then it is our duty and interest to keep up a cheerful communion with God. There are psalms proper for a wilderness, and we have reason to thank God that it is the wilderness of Judah we are in, not the wilderness of Sin. <div eID="gen11540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11541" type="x-p"/> David, in these verses, <hi type="italic">stirs up himself to take hold on God,</hi> <div eID="gen11541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11542" type="x-p"/> I. By a lively active faith: <hi type="italic">O God! thou art my God.</hi> Note, In all our addresses to God we must eye him as God, and our God, and this will be our comfort in a wilderness-state. We must acknowledge that God is, that we speak to one that really exists and is present with us, when we say, <hi type="italic">O God!</hi> which is a serious word; pity it should ever be used as a by-word. And we must own his authority over us and propriety in us, and our relation to him: "<hi type="italic">Thou art my God,</hi> mine by creation and therefore my rightful owner and ruler, mine by covenant and my own consent." We must speak it with the greatest pleasure to ourselves, and thankfulness to God, as those that are resolved to abide by it: <hi type="italic">O God! thou art my God.</hi> <div eID="gen11542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11543" type="x-p"/> II. By pious and devout affections, pursuant to the choice he had made of God and the covenant he had made with him. <div eID="gen11543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11544" type="x-p"/> 1. He resolves to seek God, and his favour and grace: <hi type="italic">Thou art my God,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">I will seek thee;</hi> for <hi type="italic">should not a people seek unto their God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>. We must seek him; we must covet his favour as our chief good and consult his glory as our highest end; we must seek acquaintance with him by his word and seek mercy from him by prayer. We must seek him, (1.) Early, with the utmost care, as those that are afraid of missing him; we must begin our days with him, begin every day with him: <hi type="italic">Early will I seek thee.</hi> (2.) Earnestly: "<hi type="italic">My soul thirsteth for thee</hi> and <hi type="italic">my flesh longeth for thee</hi> (that is, my whole man is affected with this pursuit) here <hi type="italic">in a dry and thirsty land.</hi>" Observe, [1.] His complaint in the want of God's favourable presence. He was in a dry and thirsty land; so he reckoned it, not so much because it was a wilderness as because it was at a distance from the ark, from the word and sacraments. This world is a <hi type="italic">weary land</hi> (so the word is); it is so to the worldly that have their portion in it—it will yield them no true satisfaction; it is so to the godly that have their passage through it—it is a valley of Baca; they can promise themselves little from it. [2.] His importunity for that presence of God: <hi type="italic">My soul thirsteth, longeth, for thee.</hi> His want quickened his desires, which were very intense; he thirsted as the hunted hart for the water-brooks; he would take up with nothing short of it. His desires were almost impatient; he longed, he languished, till he should be restored to the liberty of God's ordinances. Note, Gracious souls look down upon the world with a holy disdain and look up to God with a holy desire. <div eID="gen11544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11545" type="x-p"/> 2. He longs to enjoy God. What is it that he does so passionately wish for? What is his petition and what is his request? It is this (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">To see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary.</hi> That is, (1.) "To see it here in this wilderness as I have seen it in the tabernacle, to see it in secret as I have seen it in the solemn assembly." Note, When we are deprived of the benefit of public ordinances we should desire and endeavour to keep up the same communion with God in our retirements that we have had in the great congregation. A closet may be turned into a little sanctuary. Ezekiel had the visions of the Almighty in Babylon, and John in the isle of Patmos. When we are alone we may have the Father with us, and that is enough. (2.) "To see it again in the sanctuary as I have formerly seen it there." He longs to be brought out of the wilderness, not that he might see his friends again and be restored to the pleasures and gaieties of the court, but that he might have access to the sanctuary, not to see the priests there, and the ceremony of the worship, but <hi type="italic">to see thy power and glory</hi> (that is, thy glorious power, or thy powerful glory, which is put for all God's attributes and perfections), "that I may increase in my acquaintance with them and have the agreeable impressions of them made upon my heart"—so to <hi type="italic">behold the glory of the Lord</hi> as to <hi type="italic">be changed into the same image,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. "That I may see thy power and glory," he does not say, as I have seen them, but "as I have seen <hi type="italic">thee.</hi>" We cannot see the essence of God, but we see him in seeing by faith his attributes and perfections. These sights David here pleases himself with the remembrance of. Those were precious minutes which he spent in communion with God; he loved to think them over again; these he lamented the loss of, and longed to be restored to. Note, That which has been the delight and is the desire of gracious souls, in their attendance on solemn ordinances, is to see God and his power and glory in them.
entries.ef83047c25b81593ddd35f51420b47cd49e6cf30: <div eID="gen11545" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joyful Praises.</title> <div sID="gen11546" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Because thy lovingkindness <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than life, my lips shall praise thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name. <hi type="super">5</hi> My soul shall be satisfied as <hi type="italic">with</hi> marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise <hi type="italic">thee</hi> with joyful lips: <hi type="super">6</hi> When I remember thee upon my bed, <hi type="italic">and</hi> meditate on thee in the <hi type="italic">night</hi> watches. <div eID="gen11546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11547" type="x-p"/> How soon are David's complaints and prayers turned into praises and thanksgivings! After <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.2">two verses</reference> that express his desire in seeking God, here are some that express his joy and satisfaction in having found him. Faithful prayers may quickly be turned into joyful praises, if it be not our own fault. <hi type="italic">Let the hearts of those rejoice that seek the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.3">Ps. cv. 3</reference>), and let them praise him for working those desires in them, and giving them assurance that he will satisfy them. David was now in a wilderness, and yet had his heart much enlarged in blessing God. Even in affliction we need not want matter for praise, if we have but a heart to it. Observe, <div eID="gen11547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11548" type="x-p"/> I. What David will praise God for (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Because thy lovingkindness is better than life,</hi> than <hi type="italic">lives,</hi> life and all the comforts of life, life in its best estate, long life and prosperity. God's lovingkindness is in itself, and in the account of all the saints, better than life. It is our spiritual life, and that is better than temporal life, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Ps. xxx. 5</reference>. It is better, a thousand times, to die in God's favour than to live under his wrath. David in the wilderness finds, by comfortable experience, that God's lovingkindness is better than life; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> (says he) <hi type="italic">my lips shall praise thee.</hi> Note, Those that have their hearts refreshed with the tokens of God's favour ought to have them enlarged in his praises. A great deal of reason we have to bless God that we have better provisions and better possessions than the wealth of this world can afford us, and that in the service of God, and in communion with him, we have better employments and better enjoyments than we can have in the business and converse of this world. <div eID="gen11548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11549" type="x-p"/> II. How he will praise God, and how long, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.4">v. 4</reference>. He resolves to live a life of thankfulness to God and dependence on him. Observe, 1. His manner of blessing God: "<hi type="italic">Thus will I bless thee,</hi> thus as I have now begun; the present devout affections shall not pass away, like the morning cloud, but shine more and more, like the morning sun." Or, "I will bless thee with the same earnestness and fervency with which I have prayed to thee." 2. His continuance and perseverance therein: <hi type="italic">I will bless thee while I live.</hi> Note, Praising God must be the work of our whole lives; we must always retain a grateful sense of his former favours and repeat our thanksgivings for them. We must every day give thanks to him for the benefits with which we are daily loaded. We must in every thing give thanks, and not be put out of frame for this duty by any of the afflictions of this present time. Whatever days we live to see, how dark and cloudy soever, though the days come of which we say, <hi type="italic">We have no pleasure in them,</hi> yet still every day must be a thanksgiving-day, even to our dying-day. In this work we must spend our time because in this work we hope to spend a blessed eternity. 3. His constant regard to God upon all occasions, which should accompany his praises of him: <hi type="italic">I will lift up my hands in thy name.</hi> We must have an eye to God's name (to all that by which he has made himself known) in all our prayers and praises, which we are taught to begin with,—<hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name,</hi> and to conclude with,—<hi type="italic">Thine is the glory.</hi> This we must have an eye to in our work and warfare; we must lift up our hands to our duty and against our special enemies in God's name, that is, in the strength of his Spirit and grace, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.16">Ps. lxxi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.12">Zech. x. 12</reference>. We must make all our vows in God's name; to him we must engage ourselves and in a dependence upon his grace. And when we lift up the hands that hang down, in comfort and joy, it must be in God's name; from him our comforts must be fetched, and to him they must be devoted. <hi type="italic">In thee do we boast all the day long.</hi> <div eID="gen11549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11550" type="x-p"/> III. With what pleasure and delight he would praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">v. 5</reference>. 1. With inward complacency: <hi type="italic">My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness,</hi> not only as with bread, which is nourishing, but as with marrow, which is pleasant and delicious, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>. David hopes he shall return again to the enjoyment of God's ordinances, and then he shall thus be satisfied, and the more for his having been for a time under restraint. Or, if not, yet in God's loving kindness, and in conversing with him in solitude, he shall be thus satisfied. Note, There is that in a gracious God, and in communion with him, which gives abundant satisfaction to a gracious soul, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Ps. xxxvi. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">lxv. 4</reference>. And there is that in a gracious soul which takes abundant satisfaction in God and communion with him. The saints have a contentment with God; they desire no more than his favour to make them happy: and they have a transcendent complacency in God, in comparison with which all the delights of sense are sapless and without relish, as puddle-water in comparison with the wine of this consolation. 2. With outward expressions of this satisfaction; he will praise God <hi type="italic">with joyful lips.</hi> He will praise him, (1.) Openly. His mouth and lips shall praise God. When with the heart man believes and is thankful, with the mouth confession must be made of both, to the glory of God; not that the performances of the mouth are accepted without the heart (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.8">Matt. xv. 8</reference>), but out of the abundance of the heart the mouth must speak (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Ps. xlv. 1</reference>), both for the exciting of our own devout affections and for the edification of others. (2.) Cheerfully. We must praise God with joyful lips; we must address ourselves to that and other duties of religion with great cheerfulness, and speak forth the praises of God from a principle of holy joy. Praising lips must be joyful lips. <div eID="gen11550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11551" type="x-p"/> IV. How he would entertain himself with thoughts of God when he was most retired (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.6">v. 6</reference>): I will praise thee <hi type="italic">when I remember thee upon my bed.</hi> We must praise God upon every remembrance of him. Now that David was shut out from public ordinances he abounded the more in secret communion with God, and so did something towards making up his loss. Observe here, 1. How David employed himself in thinking of God. God was in all his thoughts, which is the reverse of the wicked man's character, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Ps. x. 4</reference>. The thoughts of God were ready to him: "<hi type="italic">I remember thee;</hi> that is, when I go to think, I find thee at my right hand, present to my mind." This subject should first offer itself, as that which we cannot forget or overlook. And they were fixed in him: "<hi type="italic">I meditate on thee.</hi>" Thoughts of God must not be transient thoughts, passing through the mind, but abiding thoughts, dwelling in the mind. 2. When David employed himself thus—<hi type="italic">upon his bed</hi> and in the night-watches. David was now wandering and unsettled, but, wherever he came, he brought his religion along with him. Upon my <hi type="italic">beds</hi> (so some); being hunted by Saul, he seldom lay two nights together in the same bed; but wherever he lay, if, as Jacob, upon the cold ground and with a stone for his pillow, good thoughts of God lay down with him. David was so full of business all day, shifting for his own safety, that he had scarcely leisure to apply himself solemnly to religious exercises, and therefore, rather than want time for them, he denied himself his necessary sleep. He was now in continual peril of his life, so that we may suppose care and fear many a time held his eyes waking and gave him wearisome nights; but then he entertained and comforted himself with thoughts of God. Sometimes we find David in tears upon his bed (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Ps. vi. 6</reference>), but thus he wiped away his tears. When sleep departs from our eyes (through pain, or sickness of body, or any disturbance in the mind) our souls, by remembering God, may be at ease, and repose themselves. Perhaps an hour's pious meditation will do us more good than an hour's sleep would have done. See <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Ps. xvi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">xvii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">iv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.62">cxix. 62</reference>. There were night-watches kept in the tabernacle for praising God (<reference osisRef="Ps.134.1">Ps. cxxxiv. 1</reference>), in which, probably, David, when he had liberty, joined with the Levites; and now that he could not keep place with them he kept time with them, and wished himself among them.
entries.23c994af46563763890f4d64599c560d98c0f9ec: <div eID="gen11551" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in God; David Triumphing in Hope.</title> <div sID="gen11552" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice. <hi type="super">8</hi> My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me. <hi type="super">9</hi> But those <hi type="italic">that</hi> seek my soul, to destroy <hi type="italic">it,</hi> shall go into the lower parts of the earth. <hi type="super">10</hi> They shall fall by the sword: they shall be a portion for foxes. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the king shall rejoice in God; every one that sweareth by him shall glory: but the mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped. <div eID="gen11552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11553" type="x-p"/> David, having expressed his desires towards God and his praises of him, here expresses his confidence in him and his joyful expectations from him (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">In the shadow of thy wings I will rejoice,</hi> alluding either to the wings of the cherubim stretched out over the ark of the covenant, between which God is said to dwell ("I will rejoice in thy oracles, and in covenant and communion with thee"), or to the wings of a fowl, under which the helpless young ones have shelter, as the eagle's young ones (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.4">Exod. xix. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deut. xxxii. 11</reference>), which speaks the divine power, and the young ones of the common hen (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>), which speaks more of divine tenderness. It is a phrase often used in the psalms (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Ps. xvii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.7">xxxvi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1">lvii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">lxi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">xci. 4</reference>), and no where else in this sense, except <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">Ruth ii. 12</reference>, where Ruth, when she became a proselyte, is said to <hi type="italic">trust under the wings of the God of Israel.</hi> It is our duty to <hi type="italic">rejoice in the shadow of God's wings,</hi> which denotes our recourse to him by faith and prayer, as naturally as the chickens, when they are cold or frightened, run by instinct under the wings of the hen. It intimates also our reliance upon him as able and ready to help us and our refreshment and satisfaction in his care and protection. Having committed ourselves to God, we must be easy and pleased, and quiet from the fear of evil. Now let us see further, <div eID="gen11553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11554" type="x-p"/> I. What were the supports and encouragements of David's confidence in God. Two things were as props to that hope which the word of God was the only foundation of:— <div eID="gen11554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11555" type="x-p"/> 1. His former experiences of God's power in relieving him: "<hi type="italic">Because thou hast been my help</hi> when other helps and helpers failed me, therefore I will still rejoice in thy salvation, will trust in thee for the future, and will do it with delight and holy joy. Thou hast been not only my helper, but my help;" for we could never have helped ourselves, nor could any creature have been helpful to us, but by him. Here we may set up our Ebenezer, saying, <hi type="italic">Hitherto the Lord has helped us,</hi> and must therefore resolve that we will never desert him, never distrust him, nor ever droop in our walking with him. <div eID="gen11555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11556" type="x-p"/> 2. The present sense he had of God's grace carrying him on in these pursuits (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">My soul follows hard after thee,</hi> which speaks a very earnest desire and a serious vigorous endeavour to keep up communion with God; if we cannot always have God in our embraces, yet we must always have him in our eye, reaching forth towards him as our prize, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.14">Phil. iii. 14</reference>. To press hard after God is to follow him closely, as those that are afraid of losing the sight of him, and to follow him swiftly, as those that long to be with him. This David did, and he owns, to the glory of God, <hi type="italic">Thy right hand upholds me.</hi> God upheld him, (1.) Under his afflictions, that he might not sink under them. <hi type="italic">Underneath are the everlasting arms.</hi> (2.) In his devotions. God upheld him in his holy desires and pursuits, that he might not grow weary in well-doing. Those that follow hard after God would soon fail and faint if God's right hand did not uphold them. It is he that strengthens us in the pursuit of him, quickens our good affections, and comforts us while we have not yet attained what we are in the pursuit of. It is by the power of God (that is his right hand) that we are kept from falling. Now this was a great encouragement to the psalmist to hope that he would, in due time, give him that which he so earnestly desired, because he had by his grace wrought in him those desires and kept them up. <div eID="gen11556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11557" type="x-p"/> II. What it was that David triumphed in the hopes of. <div eID="gen11557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11558" type="x-p"/> 1. That his enemies should be ruined, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.9-Ps.63.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. There were those that <hi type="italic">sought his soul to destroy it,</hi> not only his life (which they struck at, both to prevent his coming to the crown and because they envied and hated him for his wisdom, piety, and usefulness), but his soul, which they sought to destroy by banishing him from God's ordinances, which are the nourishment and support of the soul (so doing what they could to starve it), and by sending him to serve other gods, so doing what they could to poison it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1 Sam. xxvi. 19</reference>. But he foresees and foretels, (1.) That they shall <hi type="italic">go into the lower parts of the earth,</hi> to the grave, to hell; their enmity to David would be their death and their damnation, their ruin, their eternal ruin. (2.) That they shall fall by the sword, by the sword of God's wrath and his justice, by the sword of man, <reference osisRef="Job.19.28-Job.19.29">Job xix. 28, 29</reference>. They shall die a violent death, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. This was fulfilled in Saul, who fell by the sword, his own sword; David foretold this, yet he would not execute it when it was in the power of his hand, once and again; for precepts, not prophecies, are our rule. (3.) That <hi type="italic">they shall be a portion for foxes;</hi> either their dead bodies shall be a prey to ravenous beasts (Saul lay a good while unburied) or their houses and estates shall be a habitation for wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Isa.34.14">Isa. xxxiv. 14</reference>. Such as this will be the doom of Christ's enemies, that oppose his kingdom and interest in the world; <hi type="italic">Bring them forth and slay them before me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.27">Luke xix. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen11558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11559" type="x-p"/> 2. That he himself should gain his point at last (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.11">v. 11</reference>), that he should be advanced to the throne to which he had been anointed: <hi type="italic">The king shall rejoice in God.</hi> (1.) He calls himself <hi type="italic">the king,</hi> because he knew himself to be so in the divine purpose and designation; thus Paul, while yet in the conflict, writes himself <hi type="italic">more than a conqueror,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Rom. viii. 37</reference>. Believers are made kings, though they are not to have the dominion till the morning of the resurrection. (2.) He doubts not but that though he was now sowing in tears he should reap in joy. <hi type="italic">The king shall rejoice.</hi> (3.) He resolves to make God the Alpha and Omega of all his joys. He shall <hi type="italic">rejoice in God.</hi> Now this is applicable to the glories and joys of the exalted Redeemer. Messiah the Prince shall rejoice in God; he has already entered into the joy set before him, and his glory will be completed at his second coming. Two things would be the good effect of David's advancement:—[1.] It would be the consolation of his friends. <hi type="italic">Every one that swears to him</hi> (that is, to David), that comes into his interest and takes an oath of allegiance to him, <hi type="italic">shall glory</hi> in his success; or <hi type="italic">every one that swears by him</hi> (that is, by the blessed name of God, and not by any idol, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">Deut. vi. 13</reference>), and then it means all good people, that make a sincere and open profession of God's name; they shall glory in God; they shall glory in David's advancement. <hi type="italic">Those that fear thee will be glad when they see me.</hi> Those that heartily espouse the cause of Christ shall glory in its victory at last. <hi type="italic">If we suffer with him, we shall reign with him.</hi> [2.] It would be the confutation of his enemies: <hi type="italic">The mouth of those that speak lies,</hi> of Saul, and Doeg, and others that misrepresented David and insulted over him, as if his cause was desperate, <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> quite <hi type="italic">stopped;</hi> they shall not have one word more to say against him, but will be for ever silenced and shamed. Apply this to Christ's enemies, to those that speak lies to him, as all hypocrites do, that tell him they love him while their hearts are not with him; their mouth shall be stopped with that word, <hi type="italic">I know you not whence you are;</hi> they shall be for ever speechless, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.12">Matt. xxii. 12</reference>. The mouths of those also that speak lies against him, that <hi type="italic">pervert the right ways of the Lord</hi> and speak ill of his holy religion, will be stopped in that day when the Lord shall come to reckon for all the hard speeches which ungodly sinners have spoken against him. Christ's second coming will be the everlasting triumph of all his faithful friends and followers, who may therefore now triumph in the believing hopes of it.  <chapter eID="Ps.63"/> <div eID="gen11559" type="x-p"/>

entries.727eb74a01291b9bc387144850cc62ec95cbaf8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6179"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 63</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference>. The historical occasion referred to by the title was probably during Absalom's rebellion (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.23">2Sa 15:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.2">16:2</reference>). David expresses an earnest desire for God's favor, and a confident expectation of realizing it in his deliverance and the ruin of his enemies.</title> <div sID="gen9450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6179"/><hi type="bold">1. early ... seek thee--</hi>earnestly (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Is 26:9</reference>). The figurative terms--<div eID="gen9450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dry and thirsty--</hi>literally, "weary," denoting moral destitution, suited his outward circumstances.<div eID="gen9451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soul--</hi>and--flesh--the whole man (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Psa 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen9452" type="x-p"/>
entries.d53c024c1dd591d02cb8db6c36ec9bcf1c6baf09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6180"/><div sID="gen9453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6180"/>2. The special object of desire was God's perfections as displayed in his worship (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Psa 27:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9453" type="x-p"/>
entries.830bf66d344156d2255fa60446ecc49af07f5a87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6181"/><div sID="gen9454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6181"/>3. Experiencing God's mercy, which exceeds all the blessings of life, his lips will be opened for his praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.15">Psa 51:15</reference>). <div eID="gen9454" type="x-p"/>
entries.a38722c1bc7cd6cedd0819c218130b04aa69722e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6182"/><div sID="gen9455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6182"/><hi type="bold">4. Thus--</hi>literally, "Truly."<div eID="gen9455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will I bless--</hi>praise Thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.1">Psa 34:1</reference>).<div eID="gen9456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lift up my hands--</hi>in worship (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>).<div eID="gen9457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thy name--</hi>in praise of Thy perfections. <div eID="gen9458" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8e82259e1f162ced941a8f9f6e8d5c33d0a6bb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6183"/><div sID="gen9459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6183"/>5-8. Full spiritual blessings satisfy his desires, and acts of praise fill his thoughts and time. <div eID="gen9459" type="x-p"/>
entries.e37201146c3e2ffc1473f89025ee66b0c14f888c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6185"/><div sID="gen9461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6185"/><hi type="bold">9-10. those ... to destroy it--</hi>or literally, "to ruin," or, "for ruin"; that is, such as seek to injure me (are) for ruin, appointed to it (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.35.8">Psa 35:8</reference>).<div eID="gen9461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall go ... earth--</hi>into the grave, or, to death; as their bodies are represented as a portion for-- <div eID="gen9462" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad2f624d05ec9f184065262e63279132092ee388: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6187"/><div sID="gen9464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6187"/><hi type="bold">11. the king--</hi>that is, David himself, and all who reverence God, "shall share a glorious part," while treacherous foes shall be for ever silenced (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.4">Psa 62:4</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.63"/>

entries.0ad2f455c6a37ae8d2e2f540894e144959a65105: <div eID="gen20626" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20627" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20628" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20628" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20627" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20629" type="x-p"/> David's soul thirsts after God, while absent from the sanctuary, and longs to be restored to the Divine ordinances, <reference osisRef="Psa.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.63.2">Psa 63:2</reference>. He expresses strong confidence in the Most High, and praises him for his goodness, <reference osisRef="Psa.63.3-Psa.63.8">Psa 63:3-8</reference>; shows the misery of those who do not seek God, <reference osisRef="Psa.63.9">Psa 63:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>; and his own safety as king of the people, <reference osisRef="Psa.63.11">Psa 63:11</reference>. <div eID="gen20629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20630" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm is, A Psalm of David when he was in the wilderness of Judea; but instead of Judea, the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, several of the ancient Latin Psalters, and several of the Latin fathers, read Idumea, or Edom; still there is no evidence that David had ever taken refuge in the deserts of Idumea. The Hebrew text is that which should be preferred; and all the MSS. are in its favor. The Syriac has, "Of David, when he said to the king of Moab, My father and mother fled to thee from the face of Saul; and I also take refuge with thee." It is most probable that the Psalm was written when David took refuge in the forest of Hareth, in the wilderness of Ziph, when he fled from the court of Achish. But Calmet understands it as a prayer by the captives in Babylon. <div eID="gen20630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20631" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20632" type="x-p"/> O God, thou art my God - He who can say so, and feels what he says, need not fear the face of any adversary. He has God, and all sufficiency in him. <div eID="gen20632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20633" type="x-p"/> Early will I seek thee - From the dawn of day. De luce, from the light, Vulgate; as soon as day breaks; and often before this, for his eyes prevented the night-watches; and he longed and watched for God more than they who watched for the morning. The old Psalter says, God my God, til the fram light I wake; and paraphrases thus: God of all, thurgh myght; thu is my God, thurgh lufe and devocion; speciali till the I wak. Fra light, that is, fra thy tym that the light of thi grace be in me, that excites fra night of sine. And makes me wak till the in delite of luf, and swetnes in saul. Thai wak till God, that setes all thar thoght on God, and for getns the werld. Thai slep till God, that settis thair hert on ani creatur - I wak till the, and that gars me thirst in saule and body. <div eID="gen20633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20634" type="x-p"/> What first lays hold of the heart in the morning is likely to occupy the place all the day. First impressions are the most durable, because there is not a multitude of ideas to drive them out, or prevent them from being deeply fixed in the moral feeling. <div eID="gen20634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20635" type="x-p"/> In a dry and thirsty land - בארץ beerets, In a land: but several MSS. have כארץ keerets, As a dry and thirsty land, etc.
entries.b86b1b3c9741e0db08ac5d317a2dee96c8372b1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20636" type="x-p"/> To see thy power and thy glory - in the sanctuary - In his public ordinances God had often showed his power in the judgments he executed, in the terror he impressed, and in awakening the sinful; and his glory in delivering the tempted, succouring the distressed, and diffusing peace and pardon through the hearts of his followers. God shows his power and glory in his ordinances; therefore public worship should never be neglected. We must see God, says the old Psalter, that he may see us. In his temple he dispenses his choicest blessings.
entries.6d699cd90b2b4cf525c16c8b9a7100f8397945c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20637" type="x-p"/> Thy loving-kindness is better than life - This is the language of every regenerate soul. But O how few prefer the approbation of God to the blessings of life, or even to life itself in any circumstances! But the psalmist says, Thy loving-kindness, חסדך chasdecha, thy effusive mercy, is better מחיים mechaiyim, than Lives: it is better than, or good beyond, countless ages of human existence. <div eID="gen20637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20638" type="x-p"/> My lips shall praise thee - Men praise, or speak well, of power, glory, honor, riches, worldly prospects and pleasures; but the truly religious speak well of God, in whom they find infinitely more satisfaction and happiness than worldly men can find in the possession of all earthly good.
entries.3a13dcbdc62b67920f060c8afd3a0acd3ff49923: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20639" type="x-p"/> I will lift up my hands in thy name - I will take God for my portion. I will dedicate myself to him, and will take him to witness that I am upright in what I profess and do. Pious Jews, in every place of their dispersion, in all their prayers, praises, contracts, etc., stretched out their hands towards Jerusalem, where the true God had his temple, and where he manifested his presence.
entries.076fe18081f3be84b67014aad0479755890b3a2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20640" type="x-p"/> My soul shall be satisfied - I shall have, in the true worshipping of thee, as complete a sensation of spiritual sufficiency and happiness, so that no desire shall be left unsatisfied, as any man can have who enjoys health of body, and a fullness of all the necessaries, conveniences, and comforts of life.
entries.36ebb3618af5702673e5c0dc607d5b7a78d0d833: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20641" type="x-p"/> When I remember thee upon my bed - I will lie down in thy fear and love; that I may sleep soundly under thy protection, and awake with a sense of thy presence and approbation; and when I awake in the night watches, or be awakened by them, I will spend the waking moments in meditation upon thee.
entries.5200ec37ecb3f77421345123aa664197c6cffc7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20642" type="x-p"/> Therefore in the shadow of thy wings - I will get into the very secret of thy presence, into the holy of holies, to the mercy-seat, over which the cherubs extend their wings. If the psalmist does not allude to the overshadowing of the mercy-seat by the extended wings of the cherubim, he may have in view, as a metaphor, the young of fowls, seeking shelter, protection, and warmth under the wings of their mothers. See the same metaphor, <reference osisRef="Psa.61.4">Psa 61:4</reference> (note). When a bird of prey appears, the chickens will, by natural instinct, run under the wings of their mothers for protection. <div eID="gen20642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20643" type="x-p"/> The old Psalter translates, And in hiling of thi wenges I sall joy. The paraphrase is curious. "Thou art my helper, in perels; and I can joy in gode dedes in thi hiling, (covering), for I am thi bride, (bird), and if thou hil (cover) me noght, the glede (kite) will rawis me, (carry me away.")
entries.8651761e851525a895d2918178355de20927ce42: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20644" type="x-p"/> My soul followeth hard after thee - דבקה נפשי אחריך dabekah naphshi achareycha, "My soul cleaves (or) is glued after thee." This phrase not only shows the diligence of the pursuit, and the nearness of the attainment, but also the fast hold he had got of the mercy of his God.
entries.3185b078bc7f24b9676d4e779daebec4b1beace8: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20645" type="x-p"/> Lower parts of the earth - They are appointed, in the just judgment of God, to destruction; they shall be slain and buried in the earth, and shall be seen no more. Some understand the passage as referring to the punishment of hell; which many supposed to be in the center of the earth. <div eID="gen20645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20646" type="x-p"/> So the old Psalter, - Thai sall entir in till lagher pine of hell. Lahher or laigher, lower, undermost.
entries.bc10020fdf9b79b37d1e675d29e86d4abbfffea5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20647" type="x-p"/> They shall fall by the sword - They shall be poured out by the hand of the sword, Hebrews That is, their life's blood shall be shed either in war, or by the hand of justice. <div eID="gen20647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20648" type="x-p"/> They shall be a portion for foxes - They shall be left unburied, and the jackals shall feed upon their dead bodies. Or, being all cut off by utter destruction, their Inheritance shall be left for the wild beasts. That which was their portion shall shortly be the portion of the wild beasts of the forest. If he here refers to the destruction of the Babylonians, the prediction has been literally fulfilled. Where ancient Babylon stood, as far as it can be ascertained, is now the hold of dangerous reptiles and ferocious beasts. The jackal, or chokal, is a very ravenous beast, and fond of human flesh. It devours dead bodies, steals infants out of the lap of their mothers, devours alive the sick who are left by the side of the Ganges, and even in the streets of Calcutta has been known to eat persons who were in a state of intoxication. Ward's Customs.
entries.475ed021c96e16b3b86385bf208dc8dd2ad152e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20649" type="x-p"/> But the king shall rejoice - David shall come to the kingdom according to the promise of God. Or, if it refer to the captivity, the blood royal shall be preserved in and by Zerubbabel till the Messiah come, who shall be David's spiritual successor in the kingdom for ever. <div eID="gen20649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20650" type="x-p"/> That sweareth by him - It was customary to swear by the life of the king. The Egyptians swore by the life of Pharaoh; and Joseph conforms to this custom, as may be seen in the book of Genesis, <reference osisRef="Gen.42.15">Gen 42:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.42.16">Gen 42:16</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.26">1Sam 1:26</reference> : <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.55">1Sam 17:55</reference>, and Judith 11:7. But here it may refer to God. He is The King, and swearing by his name signifies binding themselves by his authority, acknowledging his supremacy, and devoting themselves to his glory and service alone. <div eID="gen20650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20651" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee has: "And the King shall rejoice במימר אלהא bemeymar Eloha, in the Word of God;" or, in the Word God; Meymar, Word, being taken here substantially, as in many other places, by the Targumist. <div eID="gen20651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20652" type="x-p"/> The mouth of them that speak lies - The mouth of those who acknowledge lying vanities, that worship false gods, shall be stopped. All false religions shall be destroyed by the prevalence of the truth. For he, Christ, shall reign till all his enemies are put under his feet. "Thy kingdom come, and hell's o'erpower: and to thy scepter all subdue." Amen and Amen.  <chapter eID="Ps.63"/> <div eID="gen20652" type="x-p"/>

entries.5525524ae0678307abcdf72adcaaa88645188d95: <div eID="gen9621" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Morning Hymn of One Who Is Persecuted, in a Waterless Desert</title> <div sID="gen9622" type="x-p"/> Now follows <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference>, the morning Psalm of the ancient church with which the singing of the Psalms was always introduced at the Sunday service.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Constitutiones Apostolicae</hi>, ii. 59: Ἑεκάστης ἡμέρᾳς συναθροίζεσθε ὄρθρου καὶ ἑσπέρας ψάλλοντες καὶ προσευχόμενοι ἐν τοῖς κυριακοῖς· ὄρθρου μὲν λέγοντες ψαλμὸν τὸν ξβ ̓ (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference>), ἐσπέρας δὲ τὸν ρμ ̓ (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.1-Ps.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>). Athanasius says just the same in his <hi type="italic">De virginitate</hi>: πρὸς ὄρθρον τὸν ψαλμὸν τοῦτον λέγετε κ. τ. λ. Hence <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference> is called directly ὁ ὀρθρινός (the morning hymn) in <hi type="italic">Constit. Apostol</hi>. viii. 37. Eusebius alludes to the fact of its being so <hi type="italic">in Ps 91</hi> (<hi type="italic">92</hi>), p. 608, ed. Montfaucon. In the Syrian order of service it is likewise the morning Psalm κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν, vid., Dietrich, <hi type="italic">De psalterii usu publico et divione in Ecclesia Syriaca</hi>, p. 3. The lxx renders אשׁחרך in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">Psa 63:2</reference>, πρὸς σὲ ὀρθρίχω, and באשׁמרות in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">Psa 63:7</reference>, ἐν τοῖς ὄρθροις (<hi type="italic">in matutinis</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen9622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9623" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is still more closely related to <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:1-8</reference> than <reference osisRef="Ps.62.1">Psa 62:1</reference>-12. Here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:1-8</reference>, David gives utterance to his longing for the sanctuary; and in both Psalms he speaks of himself as king (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, p. 56). All the three Psalms, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1">Psa 61:1</reference>, were composed during the time of Absalom; for we must not allow ourselves to be misled by the inscription, <hi type="italic">A Psalm, by David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah</hi> (also lxx, according to the correct reading and the one preferred by Euthymius, τῆς Ἰουδαίας, not τῆς Ἰδουμαίας), into transferring it, as the old expositors do, to the time of Saul. During that period David could not well call himself “the king” and even during the time of his persecution by Absalom, in his flight, before crossing the Jordan, he tarried one or two days בערבות המדבר, in the steppes of the desert (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.23">2Sa 15:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.28">2Sa 15:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.16">2Sa 17:16</reference>), i.e., of the wilderness of Judah lying nearest to Jerusalem, that dreary waste that extends along the western shore of the Dead Sea. We see clearly from <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.2">2Sa 16:2</reference> (היּעף בּמּדבּר) and <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.14">2Sa 16:14</reference> (עיפים, that he there found himself in the condition of a עיף. The inscription, when understood thus, throws light upon the whole Psalm, and verifies itself in the fact that the poet is a king; that he longs for the God on Zion, where he has been so delighted to behold Him, who is there manifest; and that he is persecuted by enemies who have plotted his ruin. The assertion that he is in the wilderness (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>) is therefore no mere rhetorical figure; and when, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">2Sa 16:10</reference>, he utters the imprecation over his enemies, <hi type="italic">“let them become a portion for the jackals,”</hi> the influence of the desert upon the moulding of his thoughts is clearly seen in it. <div eID="gen9623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9624" type="x-p"/> We have here before us the Davidic original, or at any rate the counterpart, to the Korahitic pair of Psalms, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11">Psa 42:1-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.43.1">Psa 43:1</reference>-5. It is a song of the most delicate form and deepest spiritual contents; but in part very difficult of exposition. When we have, approximately at least, solved the riddle of one Psalm, the second meets us with new riddles. It is not merely the poetical classic character of the language, and the spiritual depth, but also this half-transparent and half-opaque covering which lends to the Psalms such a powerful and unvarying attractiveness. They are inexhaustible, there always remains an undeciphered residue; and therefore, though the work of exposition may progress, it does not come to an end. But how much more difficult is it to adopt this choice spiritual love-song as one’s own prayer! For this we need a soul that loves after the same manner, and in the main it requires such a soul even to understand it rightly; for, as the saintly Bernard says, <hi type="italic">lingua amoris non amanti barbara est.  </hi>
entries.d6da0bdea552ca3a1962fddf0ed8b718d2f7e2d6: <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.3">Psa 63:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9625" type="x-p"/> If the words in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">Psa 63:2</reference> were אלהים אתּה אשׁחרך, then we would render it, with Böttcher, after <reference osisRef="Gen.49.8">Gen 49:8</reference> : Elohim, Thee do I seek, even Thee! But אלי forbids this construction; and the assertion that otherwise it ought to be, “Jahve, my God art Thou” (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.7">Psa 140:7</reference>), rests upon a non-recognition of the Elohimic style. Elohim alone by itself is a vocative, and accordingly has Mehupach legarme. The verb שׁחר signifies earnest, importunate seeking and inquiring (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.78.34">Psa 78:34</reference>), and in itself has nothing to do with שׁחר, the dawn; but since <reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">Psa 63:7</reference> looks back upon the night, it appears to be chosen with reference to the dawning morning, just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference> also, שׁחר stands by the side of אוּה בלּילה. The lxx is therefore not incorrect when it renders it: πρὸς δὲ ὀρθρίζω (cf. ὁ λαὸς ὤρθριζεν πρὸς αὐτὸν, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.38">Luk 21:38</reference>); and Apollinaris strikes the right note when he begins his paraphrase, Νύκτα μετ ̓ ἀμφιλύκην σὲ μάκαρ μάκαρ ἀμφιχορεύσω - <div eID="gen9625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9626" type="x-p"/> At night when the morning dawns will I exult around Thee, most blessed One. <div eID="gen9626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9627" type="x-p"/> The supposition that בּארץ is equivalent to כּאשׁר בּארץ, or even that the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi> (“as a,” etc.), are views that have no ground whatever, except as setting the inscription at defiance. What is meant is the parched thirsty desert of sand in which David finds himself. We do not render it: in a dry and languishing land, for ציּה is not an adjective, but a substantive - the transition of the feminine adjective to the masculine primary form, which sometimes (as in 1Ki 19:11) occurs, therefore has no application here; nor: in the land of drought and of weariness, for who would express himself thus? ואיף, referring to the nearest subject בּשׂרי, continues the description of the condition (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.25.8">Gen 25:8</reference>). In a region where he is surrounded by sun-burnt aridity and a nature that bears only one uniform ash-coloured tint, which casts its unrefreshing image into his inward part, which is itself in much the same parched condition, his soul thirsts, his flesh languishes, wearied and in want of water (<hi type="italic">languidus deficiente aqua</hi>), for God, the living One and the Fountain of life. כּמהּ (here with the tone drawn back, כּמהּ, like בּחר, <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.10">1Ch 28:10</reference>, עמד, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.11">Hab 3:11</reference>) of ardent longing which consumes the last energies of a man (root כם, whence כּמן and כּמס to conceal, and therefore like עטף, עלף, proceeding from the idea of enveloping; Arabic Arab. <hi type="italic">kamiha</hi>, to be blind, dark, pale, and disconcerted). The lxx and Theodotion erroneously read כּמּה (how frequently is this the case!); whereas Aquila renders it ἐπετάθη, and Symmachus still better, ἱμείρεται (the word used of the longing of love). It is not a small matter that David is able to predicate such languishing desire after God even of his felsh; it shows us that the spirit has the mastery within him, and not only forcibly keeps the flesh in subjection, but also, so far as possible, draws it into the realm of its own life - an experience confessedly more easily attained in trouble, which mortifies our carnal nature, than in the midst of the abundance of outward prosperity. The God for whom he is sick [<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. love-sick] in soul and body is the God manifest upon Zion. <div eID="gen9627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9628" type="x-p"/> Now as to the כּן in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.3">Psa 63:3</reference> - a particle which is just such a characteristic feature in the physiognomy of this Psalm as אך is in that of the preceding Psalm - there are two notional definitions to choose from: thus = so, as my God (Ewald), and: with such longing desire (as e.g., Oettinger). In the former case it refers back to the confession, “Elohim, my God art Thou,” which stands at the head of the Psalm; in the latter, to the desire that has just been announced, and that not in its present exceptional character, but in its more general and constant character. This reference to what has immediately gone before, and to the modality, not of the object, but of the disposition of mind, deserves the preference. “Thus” is accordingly equivalent to “longing thus after Thee.” The two כן in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.3">Psa 63:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference> are parallel and of like import. The alternation of the perfect (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.3">Psa 63:3</reference>) and of the future (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>) implies that what has been the Psalmist’s favourite occupation heretofore, shall also be so in the future. Moreover, בארץ ציה and בּקּדשׁ form a direct antithesis. Just as he does not in a dry land, so formerly in the sanctuary he looked forth longingly towards God (חזה with the conjoined idea of solemnity and devotion). We have now no need to take לראות as a gerundive (<hi type="italic">videndo</hi>), which is in itself improbable; for one looks, peers, gazes at anything just for the purpose of seeing what the nature of the object is (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.2">Psa 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.18">Isa 42:18</reference>). The purpose of his gazing upon God as to gain an insight into the nature of God, so far as it is disclosed to the creature; or, as it is expressed here, to see His power and glory, i.e., His majesty on its terrible and on its light and loving side, to see this, viz., in its sacrificial appointments and sacramental self-attestations. Such longing after God, which is now all the more intense in the desert far removed from the sanctuary, filled and impelled him; for God’s loving-kindness is better than life, better than this natural life (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>), which is also a blessing, and as the prerequisite of all earthly blessings a very great blessing. The loving-kindness of God, however, is a higher good, is in fact the highest good and the true life: his lips shall praise this God of mercy, his morning song shall be of Him; for that which makes him truly happy, and after which he even now, as formerly, only and solely longs, is the mercy or loving-kindness (חסד) of this God, the infinite wroth of which is measured by the greatness of His power (עז) and glory (כבוד). It might also be rendered, “Because Thy loving-kindness is better than life, my lips shall praise Thee;” but if כּי is taken as demonstrative (for), it yields a train of thought that that is brought about not merely by what follows (as in the case of the relative because), but also by what precedes: “for Thy loving-kindness...my lips shall then praise Thee” (ישׁבּחוּנך with the suffix appended to the energetic plural form <hi type="italic">ûn</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.7">Isa 60:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.10">Isa 60:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jer 2:24</reference>).
entries.ee72764ca0c4fdeeeeb377348a46b69f230a3149: <reference osisRef="Ps.63.4-Ps.63.8">Psa 63:4-8</reference> <div eID="gen9628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9629" type="x-p"/> This strophe again takes up the כּן (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.3">Psa 63:3</reference>): thus ardently longing, for all time to come also, is he set towards God, with such fervent longing after God will he bless Him in his life, i.e., entirely filling up his life therewith (בּחיּי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.33">Psa 104:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.2">Psa 146:2</reference>; cf. Baruch 4:20, ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις μου), and in His name, i.e., invoking it and appealing to it, will he lift up his hands in prayer. The being occupied with God makes him, even though as now in the desert he is obliged to suffer bodily hunger, satisfied and cheerful like the fattest and most marrowy food: <hi type="italic">velut adipe et pinguedine satiatur anima mea</hi>. From <reference osisRef="Lev.3.17">Lev 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.25">Lev 7:25</reference>, Grussetius and Frisch infer that <hi type="italic">spiritualies epulae</hi> are meant. And certainly the poet cannot have had the sacrificial feasts (Hupfeld) in his mind; for the חלב of the <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi> is put upon the altar, and is removed from the part to be eaten. Moreover, however, even the Tôra does not bind itself in its expression to the letter of that prohibition of the fat of animals, vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">Deu 32:14</reference>, cf. Jer 31:14. So here also the expression “with marrow and fat” is the designation of a feast prepared from well-fed, noble beasts. He feels himself satisfied in his inmost nature just as after a feast of the most nourishing and dainty meats, and with lips of jubilant songs (<hi type="italic">accus. instrum</hi>. according to Ges. §138, rem. 3), i.e., with lips jubilant and attuned to song, shall his mouth sing praise. What now follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">Psa 63:7</reference> we no longer, as formerly, take as a protasis subsequently introduced (like Isa 5:4.): “when I remembered...meditated upon Thee,” but so that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">Psa 63:7</reference></hi> is the protasis and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">Psa 63:7</reference></hi> the apodosis, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.12">Psa 21:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.16">Job 9:16</reference> (Hitzig): When I remember Thee (<hi type="italic">meminerim</hi>, Ew. §355, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) upon my bed (<hi type="italic">stratis meis</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.3">Psa 132:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.4">Gen 49:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.1">1Ch 5:1</reference>) - says he now as the twilight watch is passing gradually into the morning - I meditate upon Thee in the night-watches (Symmachus, καθ ̓ ἑκάστην φυλακήν), or during, throughout the night-watches (like בּחיּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>); i.e., it is no passing remembrance, but it so holds me that I pass a great part of the night absorbed in meditation on Thee. He has no lack of matter for his meditation; for God has become a help (<hi type="italic">auxilio</hi>, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>) to him: He has rescued him in this wilderness, and, well concealed under the shadow of His wings (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.2">Psa 57:2</reference>), which affords him a cool retreat in the heat of conflict and protection against his persecutors, he is able to exult (ארנּן, the potential). Between himself and God there subsists a reciprocal relationship of active love. According to the schema of the crosswise position of words (<hi type="italic">Chiasmus</hi>), אחריך and בּי intentionally jostle close against one another: he depends upon God, following close behind Him, i.e., following Him everywhere and not leaving Him when He wishes to avoid him; and on the other side God’s right hand holds him fast, not letting him go, not abandoning him to his foes.
entries.8d68a811f8cb48a22142dc4483e4a3ef168edb3a: <reference osisRef="Ps.63.9-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen9629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9630" type="x-p"/> The closing strophe turns towards these foes. By והמּה he contrasts with his own person, as in Psa 59:16., Psa 56:7., the party of the enemy, before which he has retreated into the desert. It is open to question whether לשׁואה is intended to be referred, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.35.17">Psa 35:17</reference>, to the persecuted one (to destroy my life), or, with Hupfeld, to the persecutors (to their own destruction, they themselves for destruction). If the former reference to the persecuted be adopted, we ought, in order to give prominence to the evidently designed antithesis to <reference osisRef="Ps.63.9">Psa 63:9</reference>, to translate: those, however, who..., shall go down into the depths of the earth (Böttcher, and others); a rendering which is hazardous as regards the syntax, after המּה and in connection with this position of the words. Therefore translate: On the other hand, those, to (their own) ruin do they seek my soul. It is true this ought properly to be expressed by לשׁואתם, but the absence of the suffix is less hazardous than the above relative rendering of יבּקּשׁוּ. What follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:10-11</reference> is the expansion of לשׁואה. The futures from יבאוּ onwards are to be taken as predictive, not as imprecatory; the former accords better with the quiet, gentle character of the whole song. It shall be with them as with the company of Korah. תּחתּיּות הארץ is the interior of the earth down into its deepest bottom; this signification also holds good in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>; Isa 44:23.<note placement="foot">In this passage in Isaiah are meant the depths of the earth (lxx θεμέλια τῆς γῆς), the earth down to its inmost part, with its caverns, abysses, and subterranean passages. The apostle, however, in <reference osisRef="Eph.4.9">Eph 4:9</reference> by τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς means exactly the same as what in our passage is called in the lxx τὰ κατώτατα τῆς γῆς: the interior of the earth = the under world, just as it is understood by all the Greek fathers (so far as my knowledge extends); the comparative κατώτερος is used just like ἐνέρτερος.</note> <div eID="gen9630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9631" type="x-p"/> The phrase הגּיר על־ידי חרב here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.18.21">Jer 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.5">Eze 35:5</reference> (<hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., not of גּרר, to drag, tear away, but נגר, to draw towards, flow), signifies properly to pour upon = into the hands (<reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>), i.e., to give over (הסגּיר) into the power of the sword; <hi type="italic">effundent eum</hi> is (much the same as in <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.18">Job 18:18</reference>, and frequently) equivalent to <hi type="italic">effundetur</hi>. The enallage is like <reference osisRef="Ps.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference>; Psa 7:2., and frequently: the singular refers to each individual of the homogeneous multitude, or to this multitude itself as a concrete <hi type="italic">persona moralis</hi>. The king, however, who is now banished from Jerusalem to the habitation of jackals, will, whilst they become a portion (מנת = מנות), i.e., prey, of the jackals (vid., the fulfilment in 2Sa 18:7.), rejoice in Elohim. Every one who sweareth by Him shall boast himself. Theodoret understands this of swearing κατὰ τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως σωτηρίαν. Hengstenberg compares the oath חי פרעה, Gen 42:15. Ewald also (§217, f) assumes this explanation to be unquestionable. But the Israelite is to swear by the name of Jahve and by no other, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">Deu 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.16">Isa 65:16</reference>, cf. Amo 8:14. If the king were meant, why was it not rather expressed by הנשׁבּע לו, he who swears allegiance to him? The syntax does not help us to decide to what the בּו refers. Neinrich Moeller (1573) says of the בו as referred to the king: <hi type="italic">peregrinum est et coactum</hi>; and A. H. Franke in his <hi type="italic">Introductio in Psalterium</hi> says of it as referred to Elohim: <hi type="italic">coactum est</hi>. So far as the language is concerned, both references are admissible; but as regards the subject-matter, only the latter. The meaning, as everywhere else, is a searing by God. He who, without allowing himself to turn from it, swore by Elohim, the God of Israel, the God of David His anointed, and therefore acknowledged Him as the Being exalted above all things, shall boast himself or “glory,” inasmuch as it shall be practically seen how well-founded and wise was this recognition. He shall glory, for the mouth of those who speak lies shall be stopped, forcibly closed, viz., those who, together with confidence in the Christ of God, have by falsehood also undermined the reverence which is due to God Himself. <reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.10">Psa 64:1-10</reference> closes very similarly, and hence is placed next in order. Invocation of Divine Protection against the Falseness of Men <div eID="gen9631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9632" type="x-p"/> Even Hilary begins the exposition of this Psalm with the words <hi type="italic">Psalmi superscriptio historiam non continet</hi>, in order at the outset to give up all attempt at setting forth its historical connection. The Midrash observes that it is very applicable to Daniel, who was cast into the lions’ den by the satraps by means of a delicately woven plot. This is indeed true; but only because it is wanting in any specially defined features and cannot with any certainty be identified with one or other of the two great periods of suffering in the life of David.  <chapter eID="Ps.63"/> <div eID="gen9632" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 63
The following psalm cannot so properly be said to consist of prayers as of a variety of pious meditations, which comforted the mind of David under dangers, anxieties, and troubles of a severe description. It contains the vows too which he made to God in the distress occasioned by the alarming circumstances in which he was placed.
A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah.
David was often compelled to flee into the remote deserts which lay in the tribe of Judah, to escape the fury of Saul. In tracing his steps, when eagerly sought after by this relentless persecutor, we find him in the forest of Hareth, and in the wildernesses of Ziph, Maon, and Engedi, all in the tribe of Judah. See 1 Samuel 22:5; 23:14, 24, 25; 24:1; and Joshua 15:55, 62. The only objection which can be made to referring the occasion of the composition of this psalm to David’s persecution by Saul is, that in the 11th verse, David is called king; whereas Saul still swayed the scepter over Israel. But, as Calvin observes on that verse, David may have called himself by this title to express his confident persuasion that God would raise him to the throne in fulfillment of his promise; and his followers might call him king even during Saul’s lifetime, though he was not acknowledged to be sovereign by any tribe till after Saul fell at Gilboa. It is, however, supposed by some that the psalm was written during the rebellion of his son Absalom, when he was under the necessity of quitting Jerusalem, and escaping into the wilderness, 2 Samuel 15:23; 16:2; and 17:29.
Psalm 63:1-4
1. O God! thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul has thirsted for thee, my flesh has longed for thee in
The Syriac, and several MSS., read כארף, ke-erets, as a land, instead of כארף, be-erets, in a land, like the parallel text of Psalm 143:6. The two letters, כ, caph, and ב, beth, may be easily mistaken for each other, differing less than the Roman letters c and g
a desert and thirsty
The Hebrew word עיף, ayeph, here rendered thirsty, is literally weary; “that is,” says Horsley, “a land that creates weariness by the roughness of the ways, the steepness of the hills, and the want of all accommodations.” He reads, “dry and inhospitable.”
land, where no water is. 2. Thus have I beheld thee in the sanctuary, to see thy power and thy glory. 3. Because thy mercy is better than life, my lips shall praise thee. 4. Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name.
 
1. O God! thou art my God. The wilderness of Judah, spoken of in the title, can be no other than that of Ziph, where David wandered so long in a state of concealment. We may rely upon the truth of the record he gives us of his exercise when under his trials; and it is apparent that he never allowed himself to be so far overcome by them, as to cease lifting up his prayers to heaven, and even resting, with a firm and constant faith, upon the divine promises. Apt as we are, when assaulted by the very slightest trials, to lose the comfort of any knowledge of God we may previously have possessed, it is necessary that we should notice this, and learn, by his example, to struggle to maintain our confidence under the worst troubles that can befall us. He does more than simply pray; he sets the Lord before him as his God, that he may throw all his cares unhesitatingly upon him, deserted as he was of man, and a poor outcast in the waste and howling wilderness. His faith, shown in this persuasion of the favor and help of God, had the effect of exciting him to constant and vehement prayer for the grace which he expected. In saying that his soul thirsted, and his flesh longed, he alludes to the destitution and poverty which he lay under in the wilderness, and intimates, that though deprived of the ordinary means of subsistence, he looked to God as his meat and his drink, directing all his desires to him. When he represents his soul as thirsting, and his flesh as hungering, we are not to seek for any nice or subtile design in the distinction. He means simply that he desired God, both with soul and body. For although the body, strictly speaking, is not of itself influenced by desire, we know that the feelings of the soul intimately and extensively affect it.
